Escalation should include:

Scope Impact Timeline Evidence Next action

docs.title: HA
docs.text: High Availability. Automatically restarts VMs after host failure.

docs.title: DRS
docs.text: Distributed Resource Scheduler. Balances workloads across hosts.

docs.title: vMotion
docs.text: Moves a running VM between hosts.

docs.title: Storage vMotion
docs.text: Moves VM storage between datastores.

docs.title: Snapshot
docs.text: Point-in-time disk state used for backup or rollback.

docs.title: Datastore Latency
docs.text: Time required to complete storage operations.

docs.title: CPU Ready
docs.text: Time a VM waits for CPU scheduling.

docs.title: Ballooning
docs.text: Memory reclamation mechanism used during memory pressure.

docs.title: Resync
docs.text: Rebuild of storage components after failure or maintenance.

docs.title: Admission Control
docs.text: Ensures enough capacity exists for failover.

docs.title: Cluster
docs.text: All hosts connected No alarms Capacity healthy

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Latency < 10 ms No failed paths No resync backlog

docs.title: Network
docs.text: No packet loss All uplinks up

docs.title: VMs
docs.text: No consolidation warnings No swap CPU ready low

docs.title: Management
docs.text: vCenter reachable Services running Backups successful

docs.title: ESXi Log Locations
docs.text:
/var/log/hostd.log       # Host daemon — VM and host operations
/var/log/vpxa.log        # vCenter agent on the host
/var/log/vmkernel.log    # Kernel-level events — storage, network, hardware
/var/log/vobd.log        # Hardware and storage event observer
/var/log/syslog.log      # General system log
/var/log/auth.log        # Authentication events

docs.title: vCenter Appliance Log Locations
docs.text:
/var/log/vmware/vpxd/          # vCenter Server daemon logs
/var/log/vmware/sso/           # SSO and identity service logs
/var/log/vmware/vapi/          # vAPI endpoint logs
/var/log/vmware/applmgmt/      # Appliance management logs

docs.title: Collecting a vCenter Support Bundle
docs.text:
In vSphere Client: Menu → Administration → Support → Export Support Bundle

Or from VAMI at https://<vcenter>:5480 → Support

docs.title: Collecting an ESXi Support Bundle
docs.text:
Via vSphere Client: Right-click host → Export System Logs

Or via SSH:

vm-support -n <bundle-name>

docs.title: Using Aria Operations for Logs
docs.text:
• Search by hostname, IP, or keyword
  • Set a time range before searching
  • Filter by log source (hostd, vpxa, vmkernel)
  • Export results as CSV for evidence or support cases

docs.title: Find All Snapshots
docs.text:
In vCenter: Menu → Global Views → VMs and Templates → Filter by snapshot state

Or use Aria Operations: Environment → VMs → filter by snapshot count > 0

docs.title: Check Snapshot Age and Size
docs.text:
In vSphere Client: Right-click VM → Snapshots → Manage Snapshots

  • Review snapshot creation date
  • Review snapshot size on disk

docs.title: Identify Snapshot Owner
docs.text:
• Check if the snapshot was created by a backup product (name will include backup job name)
  • Check if it was a manual change-related snapshot

docs.title: Remove a Snapshot Safely
docs.text:
1. Confirm the VM is healthy and the snapshot is no longer needed
  2. Right-click VM → Snapshots → Manage Snapshots
  3. Select the snapshot → Delete
  4. Monitor the consolidation task — it may take several minutes

docs.title: Consolidation Warning
docs.text: If vCenter shows a consolidation needed warning: - Right-click VM → Snapshots → Consolidate - Monitor the task and confirm completion

docs.title: Check Datastore Free Space After Cleanup
docs.text: • Confirm datastore free space has recovered after snapshot removal

docs.title: Escalate Locked or Stuck Snapshots
docs.text:
• Do not force-delete stuck snapshots without VMware support guidance
  • Collect the snapshot delta file list and vCenter events before escalating

docs.title: vCenter Service Commands
docs.text: SSH to the vCenter appliance before running these commands.

docs.title: Check All Services
docs.text: service-control --status

docs.title: Start All Services
docs.text: service-control --start --all

docs.title: Stop All Services
docs.text: service-control --stop --all

docs.title: Restart All Services
docs.text: service-control --stop --all && service-control --start --all

docs.title: Restart a Single Service
docs.text:
service-control --restart vmware-vpxd
service-control --restart vmware-sts
service-control --restart vmware-lookupsvc

docs.title: Check Disk Space
docs.text: df -h

docs.title: Check Uptime
docs.text: uptime

docs.title: Check Certificate Status
docs.text: Access VAMI at https://<vcenter>:5480 → Certificate Management

docs.title: When Not to Restart Services
docs.text:
• If disk partitions are full — free space first
  • If a restore is needed — restarting services will not fix a corrupt database
  • During active vMotion or vSAN resync operations without change approval

docs.title: Escalation
docs.text: If services do not recover after a restart, collect a support bundle from VAMI and open a VMware support case.

docs.title: VM Performance Quick Checks
docs.text: When a VM is reported as slow, check these in order:

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
• CPU Ready — time the VM is waiting for a physical CPU. Above 5% is worth investigating.
  • CPU Usage — high usage may indicate the VM needs more vCPUs or the guest application is busy.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
• Memory Ballooning — VMware is reclaiming memory from this VM. Indicates memory pressure on the host.
  • Memory Swapping — severe memory pressure. The VM's memory is being swapped to disk.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Datastore Latency — above 20ms is worth investigating. Check the storage array and paths.
  • Snapshot Age — old or large snapshots degrade VM storage performance.
  • Guest Disk Usage — confirm the guest OS disk is not full.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• Packet Drops — check the VM's NIC stats and the physical switch port.
  • VMware Tools — confirm Tools is installed and current; outdated Tools can cause NIC performance issues.

docs.title: Recent Changes
docs.text:
• Was the VM migrated recently?
  • Was the host patched or rebooted?
  • Was a snapshot taken?
  • Was a storage vMotion performed?

docs.title: Quick Commands from ESXi
docs.text:
# Check VM disk stats (run from the ESXi host)
esxtop
# Press 'u' for storage view, 'd' for disk adapter view

docs.title: Fast Health Checks
docs.text:
• vSAN Skyline Health → vCenter → Cluster → vSAN → Skyline Health
  • Object Health → vCenter → Cluster → vSAN → Virtual Objects
  • Resync Status → vCenter → Cluster → vSAN → Resyncing Components

docs.title: Common Commands
docs.text:
# Check vSAN cluster info
esxcli vsan cluster get

# Check vSAN network configuration
esxcli vsan network list

# Check vSAN disks
esxcli vsan storage list

# Check vSAN resync summary
esxcli vsan debug resync summary get

docs.title: Ping vSAN VMkernel Between Hosts
docs.text:
# From ESXi host, ping another host's vSAN VMkernel
vmkping -I vmk2 <target-vsan-vmk-ip>

# Test jumbo frames if MTU is 9000
vmkping -I vmk2 -s 8972 -d <target-vsan-vmk-ip>

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Symptom First Check Object degraded Skyline Health → check disk group and host state Resync not completing Capacity usage, network health, host maintenance state Disk group offline Physical disk health in iDRAC Network partition vSAN VMkernel reachability between hosts Capacity warning Snapshot growth, thin provisioning, stale templates

docs.title: Virtualization Standards
docs.text:
Build and operating standards for virtualization platforms.

Naming Standard Cluster, host, datastore, port group, VM, and folder naming guidance. Cluster Standard Cluster settings, HA, DRS, EVC, admission control, and baseline expectations. Host Build Standard ESXi host configuration, networking, storage, logging, NTP, DNS, and access. Datastore Standard Datastore naming, usage, capacity, alerting, and ownership. VM Standard VM sizing, tools, snapshots, tags, naming, and lifecycle expectations. Access Standard Roles, groups, permissions, break-glass access, and review cadence.

docs.title: Access Standards
docs.text:
• Use AD groups instead of direct user permissions
  • Assign least privilege access
  • Review admin access regularly
  • Remove stale accounts
  • Use service accounts for integrations
  • Document service account purpose
  • Monitor failed logins
  • Protect break-glass accounts

docs.title: Cluster Standards
docs.text:
• Use consistent HA and DRS settings
  • Enable DRS where appropriate
  • Configure admission control based on business requirements
  • Use EVC where needed for CPU compatibility
  • Keep cluster hardware consistent when possible
  • Document stretched cluster or vSAN-specific settings
  • Monitor cluster capacity and failover headroom

docs.title: Datastore Standards
docs.text:
• Clear datastore names
  • Avoid running production datastores near full capacity
  • Monitor thin provisioning risk
  • Use storage policies where appropriate
  • Remove stale ISOs and old templates
  • Review snapshots regularly
  • Document datastore ownership and purpose

docs.title: Capacity Thresholds
docs.text: Threshold Action 80% used Review growth trends 85% used Plan cleanup or expansion 90% used Open action ticket 95% used Treat as urgent — immediate action required

docs.title: Expansion and Decommission
docs.text:
• Expansion requires change approval
  • Emergency expansion process should be documented in the runbook
  • Decommission process: confirm no active VMs, remove from datastores, coordinate with storage team

docs.title: Host Standards
docs.text:
• Consistent ESXi version per cluster
  • Consistent firmware and drivers
  • Correct DNS and NTP
  • Standard VMkernel layout
  • Standard syslog configuration
  • Management access restricted
  • Lockdown mode where required
  • Hardware health monitored

docs.title: Naming Standards
docs.text:
Clear naming makes troubleshooting easier.

Object Example vCenter vcsa-prod-01 Cluster cl-prod-compute-01 ESXi Host esx-prod-01 Datastore ds-prod-vsan-01 Port Group pg-prod-app-vlan100 VM appname-prod-01 Template tmpl-win2022-standard Folder Prod / Dev / Test / Infra

docs.title: VM Standards
docs.text:
• Standard VM naming
  • VMware Tools installed and current
  • Hardware version managed
  • Snapshots should be temporary
  • CPU and memory sized correctly
  • Guest OS matches actual OS
  • Backup policy assigned
  • Owner documented
  • Criticality documented

docs.title: Critical VM Backup Policy
docs.text:
• Daily backup minimum
  • 30-day retention minimum
  • Application-aware backup where supported
  • Test restore at least quarterly

docs.title: Standard VM Backup Policy
docs.text:
• Daily or weekly backup
  • 14-day retention minimum
  • Restore test at least annually

docs.title: vCenter Backup
docs.text:
• File-based backup via VAMI daily
  • Keep at least 3 copies
  • Encryption password stored securely
  • Backup target must be off the vSAN datastore

docs.title: Snapshot Handling
docs.text:
• Backup products must clean up their own snapshots after each job
  • Alert if a backup snapshot is older than 24 hours
  • Manual change-related snapshots must be removed within 48 hours

docs.title: Backup Monitoring
docs.text:
• Review backup job results daily
  • Alert on any failed or missed backup
  • Include backup status in the weekly health check

docs.title: Backup Failure Escalation
docs.text:
• Retry failed backup once
  • If retry fails, investigate and escalate within 24 hours
  • Critical VMs with no successful backup for more than 48 hours must be escalated immediately

docs.title: Backup Evidence Retention
docs.text:
• Keep backup job reports for 90 days
  • Document restore tests with date and result

docs.title: Change Ticket Requirement
docs.text: All maintenance windows require an approved change ticket before work begins.

docs.title: Stakeholder Notification
docs.text:
• Notify all affected application owners at least 24 hours before the window
  • For critical changes, notify 48–72 hours in advance

docs.title: Window Definition
docs.text:
• Define a clear start and end time
  • Scope the window to the minimum required duration
  • Include buffer time for validation and rollback if needed

docs.title: Pre-Change Evidence
docs.text:
• Capture health check screenshots before work begins
  • Confirm backup status
  • Confirm current versions

docs.title: Rollback Plan
docs.text:
• Document rollback steps in the change ticket
  • Confirm rollback is achievable within the maintenance window

docs.title: Communication During the Window
docs.text:
• Notify stakeholders when work starts
  • Provide status updates if the window is extended
  • Notify stakeholders when work is complete and validated

docs.title: Post-Change Validation
docs.text:
• Complete all post-change checks before closing the window
  • Confirm with application owners if business validation is required

docs.title: Ticket Closure
docs.text:
• Document what was done, how long it took, and the outcome
  • Attach pre and post screenshots as evidence
  • Close the ticket with a completion note

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Document any issues or unexpected outcomes in the change ticket
  • Review with the team if the change did not go as planned

docs.title: Snapshots Are Temporary
docs.text: Snapshots are not backups. They should be used for short-term protection during changes and removed after validation.

docs.title: Approved Use Cases
docs.text:
• Pre-change snapshot during a maintenance window
  • Backup product snapshots (managed by the backup tool)
  • Temporary rollback point during a test or upgrade

docs.title: Maximum Snapshot Age
docs.text:
• Change-related snapshots: remove within 24–48 hours of change completion
  • Test snapshots: remove within the agreed test period
  • No snapshot should remain for more than 7 days without review

docs.title: Snapshot Size Monitoring
docs.text:
• Monitor snapshot size via Aria Operations or vCenter alarms
  • Large snapshots consume datastore capacity and degrade VM performance

docs.title: Cleanup Responsibility
docs.text:
• The team that created the snapshot is responsible for removing it
  • Snapshots left by backup products are managed by the backup team

docs.title: Alerting for Old Snapshots
docs.text:
• Configure vCenter or Aria Operations to alert on snapshots older than 3 days
  • Review the snapshot report weekly

docs.title: Risk of Long-Running Snapshots
docs.text:
• Snapshot files grow continuously as the VM writes data
  • Committing a large snapshot can cause temporary VM storage performance impact
  • Datastores can fill unexpectedly due to uncontrolled snapshot growth

docs.title: Emergency Consolidation
docs.text: If a snapshot cannot be deleted cleanly: 1. Check for running consolidation tasks in vCenter 2. Right-click VM → Snapshot → Consolidate 3. If consolidation fails, open a VMware support case — do not attempt forced removal without guidance

docs.title: VMware Tagging Standards
docs.text: Consistent tagging supports ownership, billing, backup policy, patch scheduling, and compliance.

docs.title: Required Tags
docs.text: Tag Category Example Values Application Owner team-infra, team-app01 Business Unit finance, operations, it Environment prod, dev, test, infra Criticality critical, standard, low Backup Policy daily-30d, weekly-14d, none Patch Group patch-group-a, patch-group-b Support Group infra-team, app-team

docs.title: Optional Tags
docs.text: Tag Category Example Values Compliance pci, hipaa, gdpr Temporary VM true (include decommission date in notes) Decommission Date 2026-06-01

docs.title: Tagging Process
docs.text:
• Tags are applied at VM creation
  • Owners are responsible for keeping tags current
  • Tags are reviewed quarterly or as part of the access review process

docs.title: Virtualization Upgrade Readiness
docs.text:
Upgrade planning, pre-checks, rollback planning, and post-upgrade validation.

Upgrade Planning Upgrade scope, dependencies, timing, owners, and risk review. Compatibility Review Version compatibility across vCenter, ESXi, vSAN, NSX, VxRail, and Aria. Pre-Upgrade Checklist Required checks before upgrade execution. Rollback Planning Rollback notes, decision points, backups, snapshots, and vendor support expectations. Post-Upgrade Validation Checks after upgrades across management, hosts, storage, networking, and monitoring. Upgrade Lessons Learned Capture issues, fixes, timing, and changes for next maintenance window.

docs.title: Compatibility Review
docs.text:
Compatibility should be checked for:

  • vCenter version
  • ESXi version
  • vSAN version
  • NSX version
  • VxRail version
  • Aria product versions
  • Backup software
  • Monitoring tools
  • Storage arrays
  • Server firmware
  • NIC and HBA drivers

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• Confirm current NSX Manager version
  • Confirm all NSX Manager nodes in the cluster are healthy
  • Confirm all Edge nodes are healthy
  • Confirm all transport nodes are healthy

docs.title: Target Version
docs.text:
• Confirm target NSX version
  • Confirm compatibility with current vCenter and ESXi versions
  • Review NSX upgrade coordinator compatibility matrix

docs.title: Pre-Upgrade Checks
docs.text:
• NSX Manager backup completed
  • NSX Manager cluster health confirmed: all nodes active
  • Edge nodes healthy: confirmed in NSX Manager
  • Transport nodes healthy: confirmed in NSX Manager
  • No critical alarms in NSX Manager
  • Confirm vCenter is compatible with the target NSX version
  • Confirm ESXi hosts are compatible with the target NSX version

docs.title: Upgrade Process Overview
docs.text:
1. Run the NSX Upgrade Coordinator
  2. Upgrade NSX Managers first
  3. Upgrade Edge nodes
  4. Upgrade host transport nodes (rolling, one cluster at a time)

docs.title: Post-Upgrade Validation
docs.text:
• Confirm NSX Manager UI is accessible
  • Confirm all Edge nodes are online
  • Confirm all transport nodes show as Up
  • Confirm routing and firewall rules are functioning
  • Confirm VM networking is working
  • Capture new NSX version for records

docs.title: Post-Upgrade Validation
docs.text:
• Confirm vCenter login
  • Confirm all hosts connected
  • Confirm HA and DRS health
  • Confirm vSAN health
  • Confirm NSX health if used
  • Confirm VxRail Manager health if used
  • Confirm Aria integrations
  • Confirm backups
  • Confirm monitoring
  • Confirm application validation
  • Check new alerts
  • Capture final versions

docs.title: Pre-Upgrade Checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm vCenter backup
  • Confirm configuration backup
  • Confirm no critical alerts
  • Confirm no failed vSAN objects
  • Confirm no active resyncs if avoidable
  • Confirm datastore free space
  • Confirm cluster HA and DRS health
  • Confirm DNS and NTP
  • Confirm certificates are valid
  • Confirm admin access
  • Confirm support bundle collection if required
  • Confirm rollback steps

docs.title: Rollback Planning
docs.text: Rollback depends on the product being upgraded. Some upgrades cannot be easily rolled back without restore or redeploy.

docs.title: Rollback Planning Should Include
docs.text:
• vCenter file-based backup
  • Snapshot guidance if supported
  • ESXi bootbank rollback option
  • VxRail support guidance
  • NSX backup
  • Aria product backup
  • Database backup if applicable
  • Clear go/no-go decision point
  • Vendor escalation path

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
After the upgrade, document:

  • What worked
  • What failed
  • Issues found
  • How long each step took
  • Vendor case numbers
  • Changes to future pre-checks
  • Updated rollback steps
  • Final validation results

docs.title: Upgrade Planning
docs.text: Upgrade planning should start before the maintenance window.

docs.title: Key Planning Items
docs.text:
• Current version
  • Target version
  • Supported upgrade path
  • Compatibility matrix
  • Hardware compatibility
  • Firmware and driver requirements
  • Backup requirements
  • Maintenance window
  • Rollback plan
  • Support contacts
  • Application impact
  • Validation checklist

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• Confirm current vCenter version and build number
  • Confirm current ESXi versions and ensure they are compatible with the target vCenter

docs.title: Target Version
docs.text:
• Confirm target vCenter version and supported upgrade path
  • Review VMware upgrade path tool: supported paths only

docs.title: Pre-Upgrade Checks
docs.text:
• vCenter file-based backup completed
  • SSO domain health confirmed
  • Certificate health confirmed — no expiring certs during the window
  • All disk partitions have sufficient free space
  • All hosts are Connected
  • No critical active alarms
  • Plugin compatibility confirmed (backup, monitoring, etc.)
  • vCenter and PSC in the same SSO domain are upgraded together

docs.title: Post-Upgrade Validation
docs.text:
• Confirm vSphere Client is accessible on the new version
  • Confirm all hosts are still Connected
  • Confirm vSAN health is green if applicable
  • Confirm NSX is functioning if applicable
  • Confirm Aria integrations are working
  • Confirm backup and monitoring plugins are working
  • Capture new version and build number for records

docs.title: VMware Platform Upgrade Procedure
docs.text: This procedure covers a full VMware platform upgrade including vCenter, ESXi, vSAN, NSX, and VCF-related components.

docs.title: Roles and Responsibilities
docs.text: Role Responsibility VMware Engineer Owns upgrade execution and validation Storage Engineer Validates datastore, vSAN, or external array health Network Engineer Validates VLANs, MTU, routing, NSX, and uplinks Backup Engineer Confirms backups and restore points Application Owner Validates application functionality after upgrade Change Owner Owns communication, approval, and ticket updates Vendor Support Assists with failures, stuck upgrades, or rollback decisions

docs.title: Capture Current Versions
docs.text:
Document before starting:

  • vCenter version and build
  • ESXi version and build per cluster
  • vSAN version and disk format version
  • NSX version
  • VCF version if used
  • VxRail version if applicable
  • Aria Operations version
  • Backup platform version
  • Storage array code version
  • Server firmware and driver versions

docs.title: Confirm Target Versions
docs.text:
• Target vCenter version
  • Target ESXi version
  • Target vSAN version
  • Target NSX version
  • Target VCF bill of materials if applicable
  • Target firmware and driver baseline
  • Target backup plugin version if needed

docs.title: Review Upgrade Path
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • Direct upgrade is supported
  • No intermediate version is required
  • Component compatibility is confirmed
  • Known issues are reviewed
  • Deprecated features and removed drivers noted
  • Plugin compatibility confirmed
  • API or integration changes understood

docs.title: Upgrade Order
docs.text:
Common order:

  1. Backup and monitoring compatibility review
  2. vCenter backup
  3. NSX backup if used
  4. VCF or SDDC Manager pre-checks if used
  5. vCenter upgrade
  6. NSX upgrade if used
  7. ESXi host upgrades (one host at a time)
  8. vSAN disk format upgrade if required
  9. Aria and monitoring validation
  10. Backup validation
  11. Application validation

For VCF environments, use SDDC Manager lifecycle order instead of manually upgrading components.

docs.title: Change Approval
docs.text:
Confirm before starting:

  • Approved change ticket with maintenance window
  • Business impact documented
  • Application owner awareness confirmed
  • Communication plan ready
  • Rollback plan documented
  • Vendor support contacts available

docs.title: Access Validation
docs.text:
Confirm access to:

  • vCenter and vSphere Client
  • VCSA Appliance Management Interface
  • SSO administrator account
  • VCSA root account if needed
  • Hardware management interface (iDRAC/iLO)
  • Backup console
  • NSX Manager if used
  • SDDC Manager if VCF is used
  • VxRail Manager if VxRail is used

docs.title: Backup Validation
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • vCenter file-based backup completed and encryption password is available
  • NSX backup completed if NSX is used
  • Aria backup or snapshot plan confirmed
  • Critical VM backups completed
  • Backup repository has capacity

docs.title: Environment Health Checks
docs.text:
Validate:

  • vCenter services healthy, no critical alarms
  • All ESXi hosts Connected, none unexpectedly in maintenance mode
  • HA and DRS healthy
  • Datastores accessible with adequate free space
  • No unexpected snapshot growth
  • vSAN Skyline Health green, no active resyncs if avoidable
  • NSX Manager cluster healthy if used
  • Backup jobs not running against target VMs
  • Monitoring active

docs.title: DNS, NTP, and Certificate Checks
docs.text:
• DNS forward and reverse lookup working for vCenter, ESXi, NSX
  • NTP synced across vCenter, ESXi, NSX, and identity sources
  • vCenter machine, STS, and solution user certificates valid
  • NSX and Aria certificates valid
  • No certificate expiring during the maintenance window

docs.title: Before Starting
docs.text:
• Run a fresh file-based backup and confirm it completes
  • Pause large VM migrations, storage migrations, bulk provisioning, and backup snapshot jobs
  • Run upgrade pre-checks: disk space, database health, service health, SSO health, plugin compatibility

docs.title: Upgrade Steps
docs.text:
1. Mount or launch vCenter installer
  2. Start upgrade workflow
  3. Deploy new appliance if required
  4. Connect to source vCenter
  5. Run pre-checks and resolve any failures
  6. Confirm network settings and appliance size
  7. Start data migration
  8. Monitor upgrade progress
  9. Log into new vCenter after completion
  10. Confirm old appliance state — do not delete until new vCenter is validated

docs.title: Post-Upgrade Validation
docs.text:
• vCenter login works
  • All services running: service-control --status
  • Inventory, hosts, clusters, datastores, and distributed switches visible
  • Permissions and tags intact
  • Plugins working
  • Backup and monitoring tools reconnected
  • No unexpected alarms

docs.title: Rollback Notes
docs.text:
Consider rollback if:

  • Upgrade fails before migration completes
  • vCenter services fail after upgrade
  • Inventory is missing or SSO is broken
  • Hosts cannot reconnect
  • Critical integrations fail

docs.title: Phase 4: NSX Upgrade
docs.text: Only perform if NSX is part of the environment.

docs.title: Pre-Checks
docs.text:
• NSX Manager cluster healthy, all nodes online
  • Edge nodes and transport nodes healthy
  • TEP connectivity confirmed
  • Backup completed
  • vCenter registration healthy
  • No critical NSX alarms

docs.title: Upgrade Order
docs.text:
1. NSX Upgrade Coordinator pre-check
  2. Edge nodes
  3. Host transport nodes
  4. NSX Manager nodes
  5. Post-upgrade validation

docs.title: Post-Upgrade Validation
docs.text:
• NSX Manager UI login
  • Edge node and transport node health
  • Segment connectivity and TEP connectivity
  • Gateway, distributed firewall rules, and routing functioning

docs.title: Pre-Checks (Per Host)
docs.text:
• Host Connected with no hardware errors
  • Cluster has enough capacity for evacuation
  • DRS can evacuate workloads
  • No VM is pinned to this host
  • vSAN resync not active if avoidable
  • Correct image or baseline confirmed
  • Firmware and driver compatibility confirmed

docs.title: Maintenance Mode — vSAN Evacuation Options
docs.text: Option Use Case Ensure Accessibility Common for planned maintenance when redundancy exists Full Data Migration Safer but slower; requires enough free capacity No Data Migration Higher risk; use only when approved and understood

docs.title: Remediation Steps
docs.text:
1. Attach baseline or image in Lifecycle Manager
  2. Stage patches if supported
  3. Remediate host
  4. Allow reboot and wait for host reconnect
  5. Confirm ESXi version and build
  6. Exit maintenance mode
  7. Validate host health

docs.title: Continue Cluster Upgrade
docs.text:
• Upgrade one host at a time
  • Watch DRS behavior, vSAN resyncs, and datastore latency
  • Pause if errors repeat on multiple hosts

docs.title: Phase 6: vSAN Upgrade
docs.text: Only perform if vSAN is used.

docs.title: Pre-Checks
docs.text:
• Skyline Health green, no failed disks, no inaccessible objects
  • No unexpected resyncs, capacity within safe limits
  • All hosts on the correct ESXi version
  • Disk groups healthy

docs.title: Disk Format Upgrade
docs.text:
Only upgrade disk format after confirming it is required and all hosts are upgraded.

  1. Confirm Skyline Health is green
  2. Confirm no active resync
  3. Start disk format upgrade
  4. Monitor resync activity and object compliance
  5. Validate vSAN health after completion

docs.title: Phase 7: Final Validation
docs.text:
• vCenter access and services
  • All ESXi hosts Connected, HA and DRS healthy
  • Datastores accessible, VMs running
  • vMotion and storage vMotion working
  • vSAN healthy
  • NSX healthy if used
  • Backup jobs running
  • Monitoring dashboards active
  • Aria integrations working
  • Application owner validation complete
  • Active alarms reviewed

docs.title: Phase 8: Documentation
docs.text:
Update:

  • Change ticket with results and screenshots
  • Version inventory
  • Upgrade notes and lessons learned
  • Support case numbers if used
  • Rollback notes
  • Next recommended action

docs.title: VMware Platform
docs.text:
The VMware platform is the core virtualization layer used to run, manage, protect, and operate virtual machines across enterprise infrastructure. The main components usually include vCenter, ESXi, vSAN, NSX, and sometimes VMware Cloud Foundation.

VMware Cloud Foundation VCF architecture, workload domains, lifecycle, and operations. vCenter Inventory, permissions, alarms, tasks, certificates, backup, and field reference notes. ESXi Host health, networking, storage paths, logs, maintenance, patching, and field reference notes. vSAN Storage policies, disk groups, capacity, resync, health, performance, and field reference notes. docs.title: Key Components
docs.text: Component Purpose vCenter Central management for ESXi hosts, clusters, VMs, permissions, templates, and lifecycle tasks ESXi Hypervisor installed on physical servers to run virtual machines vSAN Software-defined storage that uses local disks across ESXi hosts NSX Software-defined networking and security platform VCF Full-stack private cloud platform combining vSphere, vSAN, NSX, and lifecycle management Lifecycle Manager Used for patching, firmware alignment, image baselines, and upgrade compliance

docs.title: What to Know
docs.text: A healthy VMware platform depends on the relationship between compute, storage, networking, DNS, certificates, identity, and hardware health. Most VMware issues are not isolated to one layer — a VM problem may come from a datastore issue, a host issue, a network issue, or a permissions issue.

docs.title: Cluster CPU and Memory
docs.text:
• Review CPU demand vs capacity per cluster
  • Identify clusters approaching the threshold where HA failover capacity would be impacted
  • Track CPU ready — high CPU ready indicates overcommitment

docs.title: Datastore and vSAN Capacity
docs.text:
• Review datastore usage — alert when free space drops below 20%
  • For vSAN, track usable capacity and thin-provisioned risk
  • Review snapshot growth contribution to capacity

docs.title: VM Growth Trends
docs.text:
• Use Aria Operations capacity reports to forecast VM count growth
  • Review which clusters are projected to run out of capacity soonest

docs.title: Rightsizing
docs.text:
• Review oversized VMs — high CPU and memory allocation with consistently low usage
  • Review undersized VMs — high CPU ready or memory ballooning under normal load
  • Use Aria Operations rightsizing recommendations as a starting point — validate before making changes

docs.title: Monthly Review Process
docs.text:
1. Run the capacity dashboard in Aria Operations
  2. Review cluster headroom report
  3. Review datastore free space report
  4. Review top growth VMs
  5. Review rightsizing recommendations
  6. Identify clusters or datastores needing action
  7. Document findings and recommendations in the monthly capacity review

docs.title: Aria Operations Rightsizing Review
docs.text: Use Aria Operations to identify VMs that are oversized or undersized.

docs.title: Oversized VMs
docs.text:
• High CPU and memory allocation with consistently low demand
  • Review the CPU demand and memory demand charts over the last 30 days
  • Use Aria Operations rightsizing recommendations as a starting point
  • Validate with application owner before reducing resources

docs.title: Undersized VMs
docs.text:
• High CPU ready or memory ballooning under normal load
  • Indicates the VM needs more CPU or memory
  • Review trend data before increasing resources

docs.title: Resize Process
docs.text:
1. Identify the VM and its application owner
  2. Review Aria Operations recommendations
  3. Get change approval from the application owner
  4. Schedule a maintenance window if a reboot is required
  5. Resize the VM
  6. Monitor CPU ready, memory, and application performance after resize
  7. Document before and after metrics

docs.title: Monthly Review
docs.text:
• Run the rightsizing report monthly
  • Review top 10 oversized VMs
  • Review top 10 undersized VMs
  • Track progress on recommendations from previous months

docs.title: Time-Based Search Tips
docs.text:
• Always set a time range — start with the last 1 hour for active incidents
  • Expand to 24 hours or 7 days when investigating intermittent issues
  • Use the timeline view to identify event spikes
  • Cross-reference vCenter event timestamps with host log timestamps

docs.title: Aria Operations for Logs — Troubleshooting Guide
Searching ESXi Host Logs
docs.text:
Search for a specific host by name or IP and filter by log source:

  • hostd — VM and host operations
  • vpxa — vCenter agent on the host
  • vmkernel — kernel-level events
  • vobd — hardware and storage events

docs.title: Searching vCenter Events
docs.text:
Use the vCenter log source and filter by event type or keyword:

  • Login events: search SessionManager
  • Task failures: search TaskManager or error
  • Certificate events: search certificate or STS

docs.title: Common Search Examples
docs.text: Use Case Search Term Login failures Failed to authenticate Host disconnects lost connectivity or not responding Certificate errors certificate or SSL or handshake vMotion errors vmotion and error NTP issues NTP or time and drift Storage errors SCSI or datastore and error Service restarts hostd restarted or vpxa restarted

docs.title: Time-Based Filtering
docs.text: Always set a time range before searching — searching all time is slow and returns too many results. Start with the last 1 hour during an active incident, then expand if needed.

docs.title: Correlating Events Across Systems
docs.text:
When troubleshooting, search the same time window across multiple log sources:

  1. Start with vCenter events to find the first symptom
  2. Match the timestamp to ESXi host logs for the affected host
  3. Check storage or network logs if the issue involves those layers
  4. Cross-reference with Aria Operations alerts at the same time

docs.title: Exporting Evidence
docs.text: Use the export function to save log query results as CSV or text for change tickets, RCAs, or support cases.

docs.title: Certificate Inventory
docs.text:
Track the following for each Aria product:

  • Product name and version
  • Certificate subject and SANs
  • Expiration date
  • Issuing CA
  • Trust chain status

docs.title: Expiration Tracking
docs.text:
• Review certificate expiration dates monthly
  • Flag certificates expiring within 60 days
  • Confirm renewals are planned before the 30-day mark

docs.title: Trusted Root Chain
docs.text:
• Confirm the CA root and intermediate certs are trusted by all Aria products
  • A broken trust chain causes integration failures between products and with vCenter

docs.title: Replacement Process
docs.text:
1. Generate a new CSR from Aria Suite Lifecycle
  2. Submit to the CA and retrieve the signed certificate
  3. Import the certificate into Aria Suite Lifecycle
  4. Apply to the affected product endpoint
  5. Validate product health after replacement

docs.title: Pre-Change Validation
docs.text:
• Confirm current certificates are still valid
  • Confirm the CA is accessible
  • Confirm backup of current product configuration

docs.title: Post-Change Validation
docs.text:
• Confirm product UI is accessible
  • Confirm integrations with vCenter and other products are working
  • Confirm no certificate warnings in browser or product health views

docs.title: Rollback Plan
docs.text:
• Keep the previous certificate available for re-import if needed
  • If the product becomes unreachable, restore from Aria Suite Lifecycle backup

docs.title: Aria Suite Upgrade Procedure
docs.text: Covers upgrades for Aria Suite Lifecycle, Aria Operations, Aria Operations for Logs, and Aria Automation.

docs.title: Upgrade Order
docs.text:
1. Aria Suite Lifecycle
  2. Aria Operations
  3. Aria Operations for Logs
  4. Aria Automation
  5. Integrations and dashboards validation

Upgrade Aria Suite Lifecycle first if it manages the other products.

docs.title: Access Validation
docs.text: Confirm access to: Aria Suite Lifecycle, Aria Operations, Aria Logs, Aria Automation, vCenter, NSX if integrated, identity provider.

docs.title: Health Validation
docs.text:
• Product UI loads
  • Cluster and nodes healthy
  • No failed services, disk space warnings, or certificate warnings
  • Data collection active
  • Authentication working
  • Dashboards loading

docs.title: Backup and Content Export
docs.text:
Before upgrade:

  • Take supported product backup
  • Export important dashboards
  • Export custom alerts
  • Export Aria Automation blueprints and templates
  • Export extensibility workflows if needed
  • Confirm rollback plan

docs.title: Certificate Review
docs.text: • Product, vCenter, NSX, load balancer, and identity provider certificates valid

docs.title: Phase 2: Aria Suite Lifecycle Upgrade
docs.text:
Pre-check: Suite Lifecycle appliance health, repository access, product inventory sync, password and certificate locker health, disk space.

Steps: 1. Log into Aria Suite Lifecycle 2. Confirm repository access and select target version 3. Run pre-check and resolve issues 4. Start upgrade 5. Monitor request status 6. Confirm services restart and validate login

Post-check: Product inventory visible, password and certificate lockers working, environment sync working.

docs.title: Phase 3: Aria Operations Upgrade
docs.text:
Pre-check: Cluster healthy, all nodes online, data collection active, vCenter adapters collecting, cloud proxies connected, dashboards loading.

Steps: 1. Upload upgrade package or use Suite Lifecycle 2. Run pre-check and resolve issues 3. Start upgrade and monitor node upgrade order 4. Wait for cluster to come online 5. Confirm UI access

Post-check: Cluster and all nodes online, data collection resumed, dashboards and alerts working, management packs healthy.

docs.title: Phase 4: Aria Operations for Logs Upgrade
docs.text:
Pre-check: Cluster healthy, log ingestion active, disk usage healthy, agents reporting, content packs compatible.

Steps: 1. Upload upgrade package or use Suite Lifecycle 2. Run pre-check 3. Start upgrade and monitor each node 4. Confirm cluster returns online

Post-check: Logs being received, searches return recent logs, dashboards and alerts working, agents connected.

docs.title: Pre-Checks

  • Check for VMs with DRS anti-affinity or must-run-on rules
  • Confirm vSAN evacuation setting if vSAN is in use

docs.title: Entering Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
1. In vCenter, right-click the host → Maintenance Mode → Enter Maintenance Mode
  2. Select evacuation option:
  3. Move powered-off and suspended VMs (standard)
  4. Ensure accessibility (vSAN — leaves data accessible but does not fully evacuate)
  5. Full data migration (vSAN — migrates all data off the host)
  6. Click OK and monitor the task

docs.title: Monitoring the Process
docs.text:
• Watch DRS task progress in Recent Tasks
  • Confirm VMs are migrating to other hosts
  • Check vSAN resync if full migration was selected — wait for it to complete before proceeding

docs.title: Completing Approved Work
docs.text:
• Perform hardware, firmware, or patching work as planned
  • Do not extend beyond the approved maintenance window without notification

docs.title: Exiting Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
1. Right-click the host → Maintenance Mode → Exit Maintenance Mode
  2. Confirm the host reconnects and shows as Connected
  3. Wait for vSAN to rebalance if applicable

docs.title: Post-Maintenance Validation
docs.text:

  • Confirm no new alerts on the host
  • Confirm vSAN health is green if vSAN is used
  • Confirm VMs are distributed as expected by DRS
  • Confirm host hardware health in iDRAC

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: CPU Ready: < 5% normal Memory Ballooning: Should be near zero Swap: Should be zero in steady state Datastore Latency: - < 10 ms normal - 10–20 ms caution - > 20 ms problem

esxtop

docs.title: vCenter Appliance Backup and Restore Standard
Backup Configuration
docs.text:
• Use the file-based backup built into the VCSA Appliance Management Interface (VAMI)
  • Access via https://<vcenter>:5480 → Backup
  • Set a backup schedule — recommended: daily
  • Set a retention period — recommended: keep at least 3 backup copies
  • Configure a remote backup target: SFTP, FTP, FTPS, HTTP, or HTTPS
  • Set and securely store the encryption password — required for restore

docs.title: Backup Review
docs.text:
• Confirm the most recent backup completed successfully
  • Review backup job history in VAMI weekly
  • Alert if a backup has not completed within the expected schedule
  • Include backup status in the weekly health check

docs.title: Restore Requirements
docs.text:
• Encryption password must be available
  • Backup target must be accessible
  • Target ESXi host or content library must be ready to receive the VCSA OVA
  • Time to restore depends on backup size and network speed

docs.title: Recovery Testing
docs.text:
• Test a restore to a non-production environment at least annually
  • Document the restore procedure and time taken
  • Confirm SSO, services, and integrations work after restore

docs.title: Backup Evidence for Audits
docs.text:
• Export backup history screenshots from VAMI
  • Document backup target, schedule, and retention settings
  • Store evidence in the change management or audit system

docs.title: When to Restore Versus Troubleshoot
docs.text:
Troubleshoot first if: - Services can be restarted and recovered - Disk space can be freed to restore normal function - A single certificate or SSO issue can be repaired in place

Restore from backup if: - Database is corrupt - STS certificate cannot be repaired - Services fail to start after all troubleshooting steps - The appliance is unrecoverable after a hardware or VM failure

docs.title: Certificates to Track
docs.text: Certificate Location Risk if Expired vCenter Machine SSL VAMI → Certificate Management Browser warnings, API failures VMCA Root Certificate VAMI → Certificate Management Breaks all VMCA-issued certs STS Certificate vSphere Client → SSO → Certificates Login failures platform-wide Solution User Certificates VAMI → Certificate Management Service-to-service auth failures NSX Manager Certificate NSX Manager → System NSX UI and API failures Aria Endpoint Certificates Aria Suite Lifecycle Integration and access failures

docs.title: Expiration Tracking Schedule
docs.text:
• Review all certificate expiration dates monthly
  • Flag certificates expiring within 60 days — plan replacement
  • Escalate certificates expiring within 30 days — urgent action required
  • Document next renewal date after each replacement

docs.title: Certificate Replacement Process
docs.text:
1. Identify the certificate and replacement method (VMCA, custom CA, or self-signed)
  2. Confirm backup of vCenter is current
  3. Schedule a maintenance window
  4. Replace the certificate using the appropriate method
  5. Restart affected services
  6. Validate all integrations and logins

docs.title: Validation After Replacement
docs.text:
• Browser access to vCenter confirmed with no certificate warning
  • All ESXi hosts Connected
  • SSO login working for both local and AD accounts
  • Aria, NSX, and backup integrations confirmed working

docs.title: Emergency Escalation
docs.text: If certificate expiry causes a login or service failure: - Check if the local administrator account (administrator@vsphere.local) still works - Engage VMware support if SSO or STS cannot be recovered in place

docs.title: Checking Service Status
docs.text:
# SSH to vCenter, then:
service-control --status

docs.title: Disk Partition Usage
docs.text:
df -h

Key partitions to monitor: - /storage/log — fills quickly during issues - /storage/db — vCenter database - /storage/core — core appliance data

docs.title: SSO and Lookup Service Health
docs.text:
• Confirm SSO is running: service-control --status vmware-sts
  • Confirm Lookup Service: service-control --status vmware-lookupsvc
  • Confirm Identity Management: service-control --status vmware-eam

docs.title: Certificate-Related Failures
docs.text:
• Browser certificate warning usually means the machine SSL cert is expired
  • Login failures with SSO errors often point to the STS certificate
  • Check certificate expiration in VAMI → Certificate Management

docs.title: DNS and NTP Validation
docs.text:
# Check DNS from vCenter appliance shell
nslookup <vcenter-fqdn>
dig <vcenter-fqdn>

# Check NTP status
timedatectl

docs.title: Restarting Services Safely
docs.text:
Only restart services after checking disk space and reviewing recent changes.

service-control --restart --all

Restart one service at a time where possible. A full restart causes brief vCenter unavailability.

docs.title: When to Restore from Backup
docs.text:
• Corrupt database
  • STS certificate failure that cannot be resolved in place
  • Multi-service failure with no clear root cause
  • Disk partition full with no recovery path

docs.text:
• Active resyncs are normal after failures or maintenance
  • Monitor resync progress — extended resyncs can indicate capacity or performance issues
  • Avoid taking additional hosts into maintenance while resync is active

docs.title: Capacity Usage
docs.text:
• Recommended: keep usable vSAN capacity below 70%
  • Review thin-provisioned disk growth
  • Remove stale snapshots that consume vSAN space

docs.title: Network Health
docs.text:
• Confirm vSAN VMkernel adapters are active on all hosts
  • Confirm vSAN traffic is on the correct VLAN
  • Test connectivity between hosts using vmkping if network health shows errors

docs.title: Common Causes of Degraded Objects
docs.text:
• Host placed into maintenance mode without full migration
  • Disk failure
  • Network partition
  • Insufficient capacity to meet FTT policy
  • Stretched cluster site issue

docs.title: When to Open a VMware Support Case
docs.text:
• Degraded objects that do not recover after the host returns
  • Disk group failure with no clear hardware cause
  • Skyline Health showing persistent errors after corrective actions
  • vSAN objects stuck in resync for extended periods

docs.title: vSAN Resync and Object Health Troubleshooting
Checking Resync Status
docs.text:
# From an ESXi host in the cluster
esxcli vsan debug resync summary get

Or in vCenter: vSAN → Skyline Health → Data → vSAN Object Health

docs.title: Understanding Resync Types
docs.text: Type Meaning Repair Rebuilding a component after a failure Rebalance Redistributing data after capacity or host changes Evacuation Migrating data for maintenance mode Policy change Applying a new storage policy

docs.title: When Resync Is Expected
docs.text:
• Host just returned from maintenance mode
  • Disk replacement completed
  • Capacity added to the cluster
  • Storage policy changed on VMs

docs.title: When Resync Is Concerning
docs.text:
• Resync active for more than 24 hours without progress
  • Object health showing Degraded with no active resync
  • Resync blocked due to capacity or network issues

docs.title: Checking Object Health
docs.text:
In vCenter: vSAN → Virtual Objects

  • Filter by health status — investigate Degraded, Non-compliant, or Absent objects
  • Note the VM name, object type, and storage policy

docs.title: Common Causes of Degraded Objects
docs.text:
• Host removed from cluster without full evacuation
  • Disk group failure
  • Network partition between hosts
  • Capacity too low to meet the FTT policy

docs.title: Support Bundle Collection
docs.text:
If resync or object issues do not resolve after the expected timeframe:

  1. Collect a vSAN support bundle from the vCenter support bundle tool
  2. Include ESXi host logs from affected nodes
  3. Open a VMware support case with the bundle and a timeline of events

• Confirm the failed node or part with Dell support
  • Review the Dell support case for replacement guidance
  • Confirm replacement hardware part numbers

docs.title: Capture Current Node Details
docs.text:
• Hostname and IP address
  • Serial number
  • Model
  • Current firmware version
  • Cluster assignment

docs.title: Validate Cluster Health Before Replacement
docs.text:
• Confirm cluster is healthy enough to tolerate node removal
  • Confirm vSAN can maintain data availability without this node (check FTT policy)
  • Confirm no active vSAN resyncs that would be disrupted

docs.title: Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
• Place the node into maintenance mode with the correct evacuation option
  • Wait for vSAN to evacuate or ensure data accessibility before proceeding

docs.title: Dell Replacement Workflow
docs.text:
• Follow Dell's guided replacement steps from the support case
  • Confirm firmware on replacement hardware before insertion
  • Do not skip Dell iDRAC or Lifecycle Controller steps

docs.title: Validate Node Rejoin
docs.text:
• Confirm the replacement node appears in VxRail Manager
  • Confirm it joins the vSAN cluster and disk groups are healthy
  • Monitor vSAN rebalancing until complete

docs.title: Confirm vSAN Object Health
docs.text:
• Run vSAN Skyline Health after rebalancing completes
  • Confirm all objects are Healthy or Compliant
  • Confirm cluster capacity is back to normal

docs.title: VxRail Upgrade Procedure
docs.text: VxRail upgrades include VMware software, Dell firmware, drivers, and VxRail-specific lifecycle validation. Use VxRail Manager and the approved upgrade bundle — do not treat a VxRail upgrade like a standard ESXi upgrade.

docs.title: Capture Current State
docs.text:
Document:

  • VxRail cluster name and version
  • VxRail Manager version
  • vCenter version
  • ESXi version and vSAN version
  • Node models and serial numbers
  • Firmware bundle and driver versions
  • Current alarms and open support cases

docs.title: Confirm Target Version
docs.text:
• Target VxRail version and upgrade path
  • Internet-connected or offline upgrade method
  • Expected upgrade duration
  • Known issues for the target version
  • Required Dell support engagement if any

docs.title: Review Release Notes
docs.text:
Check:

  • Fixed and known issues
  • Firmware and driver changes
  • vCenter compatibility
  • Required pre-checks
  • Upgrade limitations

docs.title: VxRail Manager
docs.text:
• UI loads and communicates with vCenter
  • Services healthy, certificate valid
  • Enough disk space
  • No failed prior upgrade tasks

docs.title: vCenter
docs.text:
• Login works, services healthy
  • All hosts Connected, no unexpected maintenance mode
  • HA and DRS healthy, no critical alarms

docs.title: vSAN Skyline Health
docs.text:
• Green — no failed disks, no inaccessible or degraded objects
  • No unexpected resync, capacity within safe limits

docs.title: Hardware (Each Node)
docs.text:
• iDRAC reachable
  • PSU, memory, CPU, fans, NICs, and disks healthy
  • No predictive failures
  • Firmware inventory available

docs.title: DNS, NTP, and Backup
docs.text:
• Forward and reverse DNS working for all nodes and vCenter
  • NTP synchronized across all nodes
  • vCenter backup completed
  • Critical VM backups completed
  • Backup team aware of maintenance

docs.title: Phase 3: Pre-Upgrade Support Bundle
docs.text:
Collect before starting:

  • VxRail Manager support bundle
  • vCenter, ESXi, vSAN, and iDRAC logs if issues exist

Save with standard name:

vxrail-support-bundle-CLUSTERNAME-YYYY-MM-DD.zip

docs.title: Phase 4: Upgrade Pre-Check
docs.text:
Run VxRail Manager pre-check.

If pre-check fails:

  1. Capture failure message and detailed output
  2. Do not start upgrade
  3. Fix the known issue and re-run pre-check
  4. Open a Dell support case if unclear
  5. Attach support bundle if needed

docs.title: Start Upgrade
docs.text:
1. Upload or select upgrade bundle in VxRail Manager
  2. Confirm target version and run validation
  3. Accept upgrade plan and start upgrade
  4. Monitor each stage

docs.title: Monitor Upgrade
docs.text:
Watch:

  • VxRail Manager status and upgrade percentage
  • vCenter tasks
  • Host maintenance mode, firmware updates, and reboots
  • vSAN resync activity
  • Hardware alerts

docs.title: Node-by-Node Behavior
docs.text:
For each node:

  1. Workloads migrate off node
  2. Host enters maintenance mode
  3. Firmware and software updated
  4. Host reboots and reconnects
  5. Host exits maintenance mode
  6. Health validated
  7. Upgrade moves to next node

docs.title: Do Not Interrupt
docs.text: Do not reboot VxRail Manager, reboot hosts manually, cancel upgrade, restart services, make unrelated vCenter changes, or force remove hosts from maintenance mode — unless instructed by Dell support.

docs.title: Phase 6: Failed Upgrade Handling
docs.text:
If upgrade fails or gets stuck:

  1. Capture exact error and screenshots
  2. Review VxRail Manager status and vCenter tasks
  3. Identify affected node
  4. Check host maintenance mode state, vSAN health, and hardware alerts
  5. Collect support bundle
  6. Open Dell support case
  7. Follow Dell recovery steps

Do not guess on failed VxRail upgrades. The wrong action makes recovery harder.

docs.title: Phase 7: Post-Upgrade Validation
docs.text:
• VxRail Manager UI shows target version
  • All hosts Connected
  • vSAN Skyline Health green, no unexpected resyncs
  • Hardware health clean, firmware matches baseline
  • VMs running, DRS and HA healthy
  • Backups working
  • Monitoring tools receiving data

docs.title: Phase 8: Documentation
docs.text:
Update:

  • Change ticket with upgrade start/end time and results
  • VxRail, vCenter, ESXi, firmware, and driver versions
  • Pre-check and post-check results
  • Issues found and Dell case number if used
  • Lessons learned

docs.text:

  • Confirm no active vSAN resyncs (or they are at an acceptable level)
  • Confirm cluster has capacity to absorb the workload from this node

docs.title: Evacuation Mode Selection
docs.text:
When entering maintenance mode on a VxRail node:

Option When to Use Ensure Accessibility Standard maintenance — keeps data accessible without full migration Full Data Migration Before disk replacement or extended maintenance No Data Migration Only with Dell support guidance

docs.title: Entering Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
1. In vCenter, right-click the VxRail node → Maintenance Mode → Enter Maintenance Mode
  2. Select the appropriate evacuation mode
  3. Monitor vSAN resync if full migration is selected
  4. Wait for maintenance mode to complete before starting hardware or firmware work

docs.title: Performing the Work
docs.text:
• Complete only the approved scope of work
  • Do not extend beyond the maintenance window without notification
  • Confirm iDRAC access throughout the maintenance if hardware is involved

docs.title: Exiting Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
1. Right-click the host → Maintenance Mode → Exit Maintenance Mode
  2. Confirm host reconnects to vCenter
  3. Monitor vSAN rebalancing — this is expected and may take time
  4. Confirm vSAN object health is green after rebalancing completes

docs.title: Post-Maintenance Validation
docs.text:
• Host is Connected in vCenter
  • No new critical alerts
  • vSAN Skyline Health is green
  • VxRail Manager shows the node as healthy
  • Firmware matches the approved cluster baseline

docs.text: VxRail is part of the virtualization platform. This page is for technical operations, troubleshooting, upgrade planning, and support handoff.

docs.title: Platform Role
docs.text: VxRail is a Dell integrated HCI platform built on VMware vSphere and vSAN with Dell lifecycle, hardware, and support integration.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
• VxRail Manager
  • vCenter
  • ESXi hosts
  • vSAN cluster
  • Dell hardware
  • iDRAC
  • Lifecycle services
  • Support bundle tooling
  • Secure Remote Services / support connectivity

docs.title: Main Dependencies
docs.text:
• DNS resolution
  • NTP/time sync
  • Authentication source
  • Management network
  • Storage access
  • Certificate trust
  • Monitoring
  • Backup/recovery process
  • Vendor support access

docs.title: Ports and Protocols
docs.text: Use Protocol Port VxRail Manager UI/API HTTPS 443 vCenter HTTPS 443 ESXi host management HTTPS 443 iDRAC HTTPS 443 DNS TCP/UDP 53 NTP UDP 123

docs.title: Key Logs
docs.text:
• VxRail Manager logs
  • Lifecycle operation logs
  • Support bundles
  • ESXi logs
  • vCenter logs
  • iDRAC hardware logs

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
• Confirm management access.
  • Review current alarms.
  • Review recent failed tasks.
  • Validate DNS and NTP.
  • Confirm certificate status.
  • Check service health.
  • Check capacity and performance.
  • Confirm monitoring data is current.
  • Review recent changes.

docs.title: Useful Commands
docs.text:
df -h
systemctl --failed
systemctl status vmware-marvin
journalctl -xe
curl -k https://localhost/rest/vxm/internal/system

  • iDRAC connectivity issue
  • DNS/NTP issue

docs.title: Troubleshooting Workflow
docs.text:
1. Confirm the impact and scope.

  4. Validate DNS, NTP, authentication, and certificates.
  5. Check service status.
  6. Check storage and network dependencies.
  7. Review logs.
  8. Capture screenshots, timestamps, errors, and task IDs.
  9. Escalate with clean evidence if needed.

• Check product interoperability before upgrades.

  • Keep DNS and NTP clean.
  • Keep alerting actionable.
  • Document support ownership.
  • Avoid undocumented changes.

docs.text:
VxRail Manager notes for service health, lifecycle jobs, support bundles, connectivity, certificates, and logs.

Service Health VxRail Manager service status, UI access, alerts, and management plane checks. Lifecycle Jobs Lifecycle task review, bundle status, failed jobs, and retry planning. Support Bundles Support bundle creation, evidence capture, case attachment, and collection issues. Connectivity Connectivity to vCenter, hosts, Dell services, DNS, NTP, and support endpoints. Certificates Certificate status, expiration review, renewal planning, and service impact. Logs Useful VxRail Manager logs, collection patterns, timestamps, and case evidence.
